Dermatology · published research

Scarring alopecia

Small clinical reports describe reduced CCCA inflammation and symptoms, with some patients also reporting increased hair density. Controlled evidence and durable regrowth across scarring-alopecia subtypes have not been established.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small clinical reports describe reduced CCCA inflammation and symptoms, with some patients also reporting increased hair density. Controlled evidence and durable regrowth across scarring-alopecia subtypes have not been established.

Summary of the Evidence

Four publications are assigned directly to scarring alopecia: three uncontrolled clinical reports and one broad alopecia review. The primary reports include a 24-woman central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia cohort, a separate four-patient CCCA case series, and a 16-woman pilot split between frontal fibrosing alopecia and lichen planopilaris. No overlap between these cohorts is reported. The review also covers many non-scarring conditions, so its overall treatment findings are not direct evidence for cicatricial disease.

Human and clinical evidence

In the 24-person CCCA cohort, 21 participants were included in the reported analysis. Improvement was reported in inflammation for 61%, hair density for 57%, and symptoms for 52%. These are separate outcomes, and the study did not include a control group; concurrent care therefore limits attribution to light alone (Larrondo et al. 2025).

The four-person CCCA case series described improvement in some patients but cannot estimate how often a response occurs. In a separate 16-woman pilot, eight participants had frontal fibrosing alopecia and eight had lichen planopilaris. After ten weeks of treatment, disease-activity scores decreased in both subgroups and the number of thick hairs increased in treated areas. Counts of thin and medium hairs did not significantly change (Gerkowicz et al. 2019).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly addressing scarring alopecia was identified in this category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell-culture study is reported. A separate lichen planopilaris biopsy analysis found no significant gene-expression change in its low-level-light arm; the result concerns one subtype.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The mixed FFA/LPP pilot used 630-nm red visible light from a superluminescent diode, at 70 mW/cm² and 44.45 J/cm² once weekly for ten weeks. The newer CCCA cohort used a wearable red-light cap, but complete dosimetry is not available in the database record. There is no dose-finding comparison, and results from different subtypes and delivery devices cannot identify one preferred regimen.

Interpretation

The strongest clinical observations are reductions in reported CCCA inflammation and symptoms, with increased hair density noted in some participants. Those findings support further study of light as an adjunct, but regrowth and durability remain uncertain. Results in one scarring-alopecia subtype should not be assumed to apply to the others.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term reduction in CCCA inflammation and symptoms Very low for durable hair regrowth across scarring alopecia subtypes
Publications and records4 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The CCCA cohort and smaller FFA/LPP reports describe lower inflammation, symptoms, or disease activity, but none used an untreated or sham comparison and some participants continued other care. Hair regrowth was not consistently measured. A replicated controlled trial with objective hair counts, stable background therapy, subtype-specific outcomes, and follow-up after treatment would support a stronger assessment.
